title: Bible Study Coffee
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
BARMATRIX Q#: 14668_bible_study_coffee

A common law jurisdiction defines first-degree murder as any murder that is (1) committed by means of poison or (2) premeditated. All other murder is second-degree murder, and manslaughter is defined as at common law.

Lydia was angry with Peter, the volunteer coordinator for a church bake-sale team, because Peter refused to give her the lead role at the dessert table. Intending to cause Peter discomfort, Lydia secretly dropped into Peter’s coffee three over-the-counter laxative pills. Peter drank the coffee containing the pills. Although the pills would not have been dangerous to an ordinary person, because Peter was already taking other medication, he suffered a seizure and died.

If Lydia is charged with murder in the first degree, should she be convicted?
call: If Lydia is charged with murder in the first degree, should she be convicted?

choices.A: Yes, only because she used poison.
choices.B: Yes, only because she acted with premeditation.
choices.C: Yes, both because she used poison and because she acted with premeditation.

rightExplanation:
D is correct.

Gold Key: First-degree-murder facts do not matter until there is murder. Poison and premeditation are degree elevators; they do not replace malice. Here, Lydia intended discomfort, not death or serious bodily injury, and the ordinary laxatives were not dangerous to an ordinary person. The unusual medication reaction caused death, but the facts do not show the malice needed for murder. So she should not be convicted of first-degree murder.

Silver Key: When three choices all say “Yes” by arguing different first-degree elevators, and the fourth says “No,” check the murder threshold before debating degree. If the threshold fails, all elevator choices fall together.

wrongExplanations.A: A is the dominant trap. It treats the laxative tablets as “poison.” Gold Key: The poison label is not enough unless there is murder with malice, and the facts also say the pills were ordinary OTC laxatives not dangerous to an ordinary person. This choice over-upgrades a discomfort prank into first-degree murder.
wrongExplanations.B: B confuses planning the act with premeditating a killing. Lydia planned to cause discomfort. The stem does not show an intent to kill or seriously injure Peter. Silver Key: do not let “she planned something” become “she premeditated murder.”.
wrongExplanations.C: C stacks both bad upgrades. The poison branch fails, and the premeditation branch fails. More important, both are degree arguments that presuppose murder. The threshold murder problem remains.

c3.label: CUT / CALL hybrid
c3.text:
The answer array offers three “Yes” upgrade choices and one “No” threshold choice.

* A: cut as flat_misstatement / NOT_TRUE. It calls ordinary OTC laxatives “poison” for the first-degree elevator.
* B: cut as wrong_element / NOT_RESPONSIVE. It proves planned discomfort, not premeditated killing.
* C: cut as flat_misstatement / NOT_TRUE. It compounds two unsupported first-degree elevator labels.
* D: residual. It answers the actual threshold: no murder, so no first-degree murder.

studentScript: Poison/premeditation are upgrades. First ask murder. Intent was discomfort; pills were ordinary and not dangerous to an ordinary person. No malice. No first-degree murder. Pick D.

A.signal: The stem says ordinary OTC laxatives, not dangerous to an ordinary person.
A.lawyer: A fails because the method is not the poison elevator on these facts and, independently, there is no murder threshold because malice is absent.

B.signal: The stem gives intent to cause discomfort, not intent to kill.
B.lawyer: Premeditation for first-degree murder means premeditated killing, not merely premeditated administration of a nondeadly discomfort-causing substance.

C.signal: It stacks both first-degree labels, but the stem supports neither.
C.lawyer: C fails because the poison label and premeditated-killing label both fail, and because the killing is not murder absent malice.

D.signal: All Yes choices are degree upgrades; D is the only threshold answer.
D.lawyer: D is correct because the facts do not show malice aforethought and therefore do not establish murder of any degree.

goldKeys.statement: First-degree murder still starts with murder. Poison or premeditation can upgrade a murder, but they do not replace malice.
goldKeys.trigger: answer choices debate first-degree labels while the stem gives only intent to cause discomfort

silverKeys.statement: When three choices say Yes by naming first-degree labels and one says No, check the murder threshold before grading degree.
silverKeys.trigger: choices A/B/C are poison, premeditation, both; choice D is No

remediation.title: Murder threshold before murder degree
remediation.signal: The answer choices argue poison, premeditation, both, or no.
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the facts show murder with malice before choosing a degree label.
remediation.tinyRule: No malice, no murder; no murder, no first-degree murder.
remediation.trap: Treating first-degree labels as substitutes for malice.
